source: Jamrozik & Gentner (2020) Relational labeling unlocks inert knowledge. Cognition 196:104146
finding: Theory: relations are encoded variably across situations, objects uniformly. So memory retrieval favours shared objects or domain over shared relational structure. A relational schema label (for example 'inoculation') invites one uniform relational construal and so raises relational reminding.
numbers: Cued-recall paradigm: study 14 passages (10 test, 4 filler), 15-min filler, then new passages sharing relational structure with one old passage and domain with another. A label was one added sentence: 'This is an example of inoculation'.
limits: Lab study of US undergraduates; known relation terms; text passages, not agent runs.
agent_relevance: Naming the relation is a cheap cue for analogical retrieval. Supports S2 (name the relation) before retrieving prior cases.

source: Jamrozik & Gentner (2020) Relational labeling unlocks inert knowledge. Cognition 196:104146 - Exp 1 baseline
finding: With no labels, people retrieved far more same-domain matches than relational matches.
numbers: Exp 1 N=251 (36 per condition, 7 conditions). Baseline: 4.58 of 10 domain matches vs 1.56 of 10 relational matches.
limits: Same stimulus sets throughout.
agent_relevance: Default retrieval (also text-similarity memory) favours surface matches; plan for it.

source: Jamrozik & Gentner (2020) Relational labeling unlocks inert knowledge. Cognition 196:104146 - Exp 1 label effect
finding: Relational labels raised relational retrieval and lowered domain retrieval. Labels at both encoding and test worked best; labels at test alone worked only when placed before the test passage.
numbers: Relational matches out of 10 (Poisson estimates): baseline 1.56; encoding label before passage 3.19; after 3.40; test label before 2.51; test label after 1.97 (p=.188, n.s.); encoding+test before 5.67; after 6.78. Bayes factor vs intercept-only 2.45e26. Domain matches fell from 4.58 to 2.53 and 2.80 (encoding) and 2.25 and 1.89 (both).
limits: With labels in both phases, part of the gain may be a plain word match, not a relational construal (the authors say so).
agent_relevance: Label both the stored case and the query with the same relation term. Put the label before the problem text.

source: Jamrozik & Gentner (2020) Relational labeling unlocks inert knowledge. Cognition 196:104146 - Exp 2 relational vs domain labels
finding: Domain labels (for example 'this is an example from anatomy') did not help domain retrieval and did not help relational retrieval. Relational labels did, replicating Exp 1.
numbers: Exp 2 N=114 (17 per condition), labels all before passage. Relational matches: baseline 2.44; encoding label 4.33; test label 4.53; both 4.21 (about 1.8 times baseline). Domain-label models: Bayes factor below 1 (0.389 for domain matches, 0.301 for relational matches), so the intercept-only model was preferred.
limits: One stimulus set (10 relational patterns); ceiling check was by total responses only.
agent_relevance: Relation names do work that topic tags do not. Do not swap topic keywords in for relation names.

source: Jamrozik & Gentner (2020) Relational labeling unlocks inert knowledge. Cognition 196:104146 - alternative accounts
finding: Authors list competing explanations: local salience of the named relation, self-generated labels, lexical cue. They argue the domain-label null weakens the salience account but do not rule it out.
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Clement, Mawby & Giles (1994): same or synonymous verbs for analogous cases improve relational retrieval; Ripoll (1998): a domain title did not help without surface cues.
limits: Alternatives not fully ruled out.
agent_relevance: When testing relation labels in prompts, include a pseudo-label control to separate meaning from lexical overlap.

source: Bassok, Chase & Martin (1998) as reported in Jamrozik & Gentner (2020)
finding: People alter a requested arithmetic operation to fit the objects named, so relation encoding depends on content.
numbers: Addition problems were accurate 82% for symmetrical pairs (tulips-daffodils) but 61% for asymmetric pairs (tulips-vases).
limits: Second-hand: read in the 2020 paper; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Content can pull a model off the intended relation; name the operation explicitly and check it on the answer.

source: Gentner & France (1988) verb mutability as reported in Jamrozik & Gentner (2020)
finding: When asked to paraphrase strained sentences ('The car worshipped'), people change the verb meaning far more than the noun meaning. Relational terms are more mutable than entity terms.
numbers: No numbers in the text read.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Relation words shift with context, so a relation label needs a stated definition in the prompt.

source: Lupyan (2012) Linguistically modulated perception and cognition: the label-feedback hypothesis. Front. Psychol. 3:54
finding: Label-feedback hypothesis: language is not a separate channel. A word, once active, feeds back and changes perceptual and conceptual activation online. This explains deep effects that are also easy to disrupt with verbal interference.
numbers: Argument plus a small connectionist simulation (PCA of perceptual layers learned with the label as network output vs no label); typicality interacts with labels.
limits: Mostly entity categories and perception, not relations. Simulation is small scale.
agent_relevance: Words in context act as live modulators of processing, not only storage. Naming a relation mid-reasoning should shift what is attended.

source: Lupyan, Rakison & McClelland (2007) as described in Lupyan (2012)
finding: Redundant labels sped learning of novel categories. Participants learned 16 'aliens' (approach vs avoid) faster when each trial also gave a nonsense label ('leebish', 'grecious'). Equally redundant non-linguistic cues (where the alien lives) did not help. Label learners kept their accuracy in a later no-feedback test; no-label learners declined.
numbers: Review gives no sample sizes.
limits: Described in the 2012 review; primary not opened. Entity categories, not relations.
agent_relevance: A symbolic tag is different from an extra metadata field; labels add value beyond being features.

source: Lupyan & Spivey (2010) as described in Lupyan (2012)
finding: Hearing the redundant word 'five' before a display sped (and sometimes sharpened) attention to 5s among 2s. The effect is transient: gone if the word came more than 1600 ms before the display.
numbers: Items shown 100 ms; 45-min experiment; word on randomly mixed trials.
limits: Described in the review. Short time window.
agent_relevance: A label must sit close to where it is used; recency in the context matters.

source: Lupyan & Spivey (2008) as described in Lupyan (2012)
finding: Telling people that novel shapes were rotated 2s and 5s dramatically improved visual-search reaction times for those shapes.
numbers: Review gives no numbers.
limits: Described only.
agent_relevance: One sentence naming a pattern can change how unfamiliar input is processed.

source: Lupyan (2012) - boundary and dispute
finding: The review notes that fast or brief label effects (Boroditsky 2001; January & Kako 2007) were used by critics to call them shallow, and that colour-space claims are disputed (Witzel & Gegenfurtner footnote).
numbers: Not numeric.
limits: Perception claims remain contested.
agent_relevance: Do not over-claim: label help depends on category variability and fades when entrenched.

source: Anderson, Chang, Hespos & Gentner (2022) No evidence for language benefits in infant relational learning - Exp 1 relational labels
finding: Failed extension. 12-month-olds heard 'These are same/different' on three pairs before habituation. No relational-label benefit; infants did not discriminate on relational-label trials or pair-habituation trials.
numbers: N=64 analysed (33 same, 31 different). Relational Label trials F(1,60)<1, p=.354; 34 of 64 looked longer at novel. Pair Habituation F(1,57)<1, p=.636. Versus Ferry et al. 2015 no-label study: F(1,121)=5.05, p=.026 (Ferry infants 18.31 s vs 13.21 s; these 16.60 vs 16.05 s).
limits: Only 3 labelled examples; 'These are same' is ungrammatical; no Bayes factors; near-threshold post hoc tests. Authors blame age and slow relational vocabulary.
agent_relevance: Boundary: relation words help only if the learner already knows what they mean. An ungrounded label adds nothing.

source: Anderson, Chang, Hespos & Gentner (2022) No evidence for language benefits in infant relational learning - Exp 2 object labels
finding: Object labels ('This is a cup') did not help and may have disrupted relational processing, matching the salient-object pattern in Ferry et al. 2015.
numbers: N=48. Object Label trials F(1,43)<1, p=.75; Pair Habituation F(1,43)=3.89, p=.055, with condition interaction F=7.59, p=.009. Object label vs salient-object comparison F(1,105)<1, p=.837.
limits: Label and salience are confounded.
agent_relevance: Naming objects can pull attention to entities and away from relations; keep entity labels out of relation steps.

source: Rattermann & Gentner (1998), Christie & Gentner (2014), Hoyos et al. (2016) as reported in Anderson et al. (2022)
finding: Labelling objects 'daddy, mommy, baby' raised relational matches in 3-year-olds; relational labels helped 3-year-olds pass relational match-to-sample; naming objects before that task impaired 4-year-olds.
numbers: Rattermann & Gentner 1998: relational matches rose from 32% to 79% in 3-year-olds (as reported).
limits: Second-hand figures; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Relational labels give young learners a handle on relations; labels on entities can hurt.

source: Zheng, Goldwater & Gentner (2025) Structural alignment and linguistic contrast help children learn a key principle of spatial construction. Cognitive Science - Exp 1
finding: Children shown braced vs unbraced buildings learned 'a diagonal brace gives stability' better with a highly alignable training pair and with a contrastive brace label. The label helped transfer but not the immediate repair task.
numbers: N=64 children aged 5-7, 16 per cell, 2x2 alignment x label. Repair: alignment b=1.661, p=.003 (OR 2.31); language b=0.304, p=.58. Transfer: alignment b=1.938, p=.005 (OR 2.66); language b=2.278, p=.001 (OR 3.15). No alignment x language interaction.
limits: Between-subjects; one engineering concept; the word 'brace' used casually, never explained.
agent_relevance: A named part of the structure supports transfer even without explicit compare instructions.

source: Zheng, Goldwater & Gentner (2025) Structural alignment and linguistic contrast help children learn a key principle of spatial construction. Cognitive Science - Exp 2 delayed
finding: Benefits of alignment and label persisted 2-5 days. The label effect was significant on every measure including the hardest far-transfer construction task, where alignment was not.
numbers: Final N=116 (29 per cell; 15 lost to no-return, 5 failed memory check). Label odds ratios: Day-1 repair 1.55 (p=.032), Day-2 repair 1.76 (p=.012), near transfer 2.57 (p=.001), far construction 1.60 (p=.027), far recognition 1.75 (p=.007). Alignment far construction OR 1.36, p=.15.
limits: Alignment x label interactions inconsistent: labelling shrank the alignment gap only for near transfer (ceiling) and enlarged it for far construction. Ages 5-7 only.
agent_relevance: A label gives durable retention of a relational insight; cheap to add to a stored lesson.

source: Loewenstein & Gentner (2001) model-room study as reported in Zheng et al. (2025)
finding: Comparing two near-identical rooms before a search task raised correct choices on twin objects, showing children then used spatial relations, not object matches.
numbers: Comparison group over 70% correct on twin objects vs 42% control; memory of the original hiding place 83%.
limits: Second-hand; 3.5-year-olds; tests comparison, not language.
agent_relevance: The Gentner recipe: compare cases first, then name the shared relation.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) - homesign link
finding: Cited evidence: homesigners, who lack conventional spatial relation terms, expressed objects and actions as often as hearing children but far less often spatial relations (in, on, under, top, bottom). Late sign exposure did not predict spatial memory (Karadoller et al. 2022).
numbers: No numbers in the text read.
limits: Mixed evidence on whether language causes spatial skill.
agent_relevance: Relation vocabulary availability tracks relation expression; causal direction still debated.

source: Zettersten, Bredemann, Kaul, Ellis, Lupyan et al. (2024) Nameability supports rule-based category learning in children and adults. Child Development 95(2):497-514
finding: Easy-to-name features (red, brown) make a category rule easier to find than hard-to-name ones (mauve, sienna). Adults benefited more than children. Children who knew hard colour words learned better when those colours defined the rule.
numbers: Children N=97 (ages 4-6); adults N=90. Adults 95.8% vs 87.3% (d=1.06, p<.001). Children 71.0% vs 65.9% overall (p=.118, n.s.) but condition x block p=.010; last block of round 1 74.2% vs 63.3% (d=0.57). Generalisation phase: no nameability effect (adults p=.91, children p=.33). Vocabulary link in children b=.05, p=.009.
limits: Vocabulary link is correlational; familiarity not separated from nameability; not preregistered; colour only; names as hypotheses, not relations.
agent_relevance: Mechanism: words supply compact hypotheses. Supports offering named candidate rules, but the effect did not carry to no-feedback generalisation.

source: Gerson & Woodward (2014) Labels facilitate infants' comparison of action goals (listed only)
finding: Search hit only: the title says labels help infants compare action goals. Contrasts with the Anderson 2022 null for same/different at 12 months.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Pointer for Angle B.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour - matrices
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on novel text-digit matrix problems, zero-shot, with no relation labels given.
numbers: Humans N=40. GPT-3 vs humans: generation OR=1.88, p=.005; multiple choice OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8.
limits: Digit Matrices built to be novel; later work questions generality (Lewis & Mitchell).
agent_relevance: LLMs can map relations unnamed, but the result is fragile.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour - story analogies
finding: On analogies between stories that share causal relations, GPT-3 beat chance on near analogies but not far analogies. Humans did well on both. GPT-4 looked stronger in a pilot.
numbers: Humans N=54. Near: GPT-3 binomial p=.0039. Far: GPT-3 p=.065. Humans better overall: GPT-3 OR=0.37, p=.0003. 15 of 54 humans picked the analogous story on every trial.
limits: No labelling manipulation was run.
agent_relevance: Far, relation-only matching was the weak spot of 2023 models; this is where S2 relation naming could help. Untested here.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets: humans stay high; GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 drop sharply. Many model errors followed an alternate rule instead of the stated successor order.
numbers: Human accuracy was significantly above every GPT model across counterfactual alphabets (95% binomial CIs, their Table 2). Error table shows alternate-rule errors in 38.59%, 22% and 5.81% of errors for different rows, about 15% for humans in another category.
limits: Exact per-model mapping of table rows not recoverable from extracted text; counts approximate. 2023 model versions.
agent_relevance: Models lean on familiar content. Stating the relation name and the new mapping rule is a plausible fix, not tested in this paper.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners. ICLR 2024
finding: Prompting the model to recall relevant problems (and for code, write a tutorial) before solving beats 0-shot CoT and fixed 3-shot CoT. This is self-generated case retrieval, not relation labelling.
numbers: GSM8K GPT3.5-turbo: about 75.0% (0-shot CoT), 75.8% (3-shot CoT), 77.8% self-generated exemplars. BIG-Bench: word sorting 66.8% (0-shot) to 75.2%; logical deduction (five objects) 30.0% to 41.6%; temporal sequences 3-shot 58.0% vs 57.6%. Codeforces Acc@1: GPT3.5 15% vs GPT-4 16% (knowledge+exemplars).
limits: Table row alignment partly guessed from extracted text; check before quoting. Gains small on GSM8K.
agent_relevance: Supports a recall-then-solve step. Natural test: ask for the relation name first, then the exemplars.
